I'm 54 years old and I've been farming these plots for 30 years, ever since my father handed them over to me. I finished middle school, so I can read the fertilizer bags and I remember some of what the extension agent said about balanced fertilization, but honestly I trust my own eyes more than what some young technician tells me. I know every corner of these 10.9 mu — where the soil is a bit heavier, where it dries out faster, and which field got flooded in 2021.

We have 11 people in the household: my wife and me, my elderly mother, my two sons and their wives, and three grandchildren. My two sons work in a factory in Handan most of the year, so they're not around for farm work except maybe at wheat harvest if they can get leave. That leaves me, my wife, and my daughters-in-law for the day-to-day work. We don't hire much labor because money is tight — my sons send home about 5,000 yuan a year, which helps, but I still need cash for my mother's blood pressure medicine and the grandchildren's school fees.

I split the land into two parts: 8 mu in the wheat-maize rotation — that's our bread and butter, feeds the family and brings cash income — and 2.9 mu near the house in cotton. The cotton field has been cotton for as long as I can remember. My wife likes it because she can pick it bit by bit between looking after the grandchildren, and the cotton income usually pays for the children's school uniforms and books.

For the wheat I planted last October on the 8 mu, I used a local improved variety, not the most expensive hybrid seed but one that does well here. I put down compound fertilizer as base before planting — about 50 kg per mu — and then topdressed with urea at green-up in March. Now it's late April and the wheat is heading. I'll irrigate once more at grain filling if the weather stays dry, and I'll spray fungicide if I see any rust. I learned my lesson in 2016 when I skipped the fungicide and lost two dan per mu. I expect about 420 kg per mu if the weather holds — last year I got 400, and the soil looks about the same.

For maize, I'll plant immediately after wheat harvest in mid-June. There's no time for tillage — the window is less than a week. I'll hire the custom planter to no-till seed straight into the wheat stubble. I have to buy hybrid seed every year, which costs more than saving my own, but the yield difference pays for itself. I'll put down fertilizer with the planter and probably topdress once more at the big trumpet stage if the plants look hungry. Two irrigations should be enough in summer — July and August usually bring some rain, and I don't want to pay for pumping more than I have to. I'm hoping for 480 kg per mu, maybe 500 if it's a wet summer.

The cotton on the 2.9 mu gets planted in the next few days, before the end of April. I use less fertilizer on cotton than on grain — maybe 12 kg of nitrogen per mu total, half at planting and half at flowering. Cotton needs more pesticide because of the bollworm; I'll spray insecticide three or four times and use herbicide once. Two irrigations, one at flowering and one at boll stage. With family picking through September and October, I should get about 260 kg of lint per mu.

Why these numbers? Because I can't afford more. If I had extra cash, sure, maybe I'd put another 5 kg of urea on the wheat, but I need to keep a reserve. My rule is: don't spend the last yuan in your pocket on fertilizer. I'd rather apply slightly too much than too little on the wheat — a bad wheat year means we buy grain from the market, which hurts more than a good year helps. But I'm not wasteful. I've tried high fertilizer rates on maize before and the extra yield didn't cover the cost when the price dropped to 1.1 yuan per jin. So I aim for "good enough," not maximum.

Total input costs will run about 4,560 yuan this year. That's a big chunk, but manageable with my sons' remittances. If they hadn't sent money home last month, I'd probably cut back to 10 kg of nitrogen on the cotton and skip the maize topdress.
